title: The House at Jorasanko: the School in the Mango Grove, the Prize Read Out in His Absence, and the Terrace at San Isidro
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Jorasanko, and the Road North with His Father

stops.name: Jorasanko Thakur Bari, Calcutta: the youngest son
stops.date_confidence: attested. English Wikipedia, 'Rabindranath Tagore' and 'Jorasanko Thakur Bari', agree on 7 May 1861 and on the parents. The pin is corrected: the research pool's chronology lens carried 22.5958, 88.3639, which sits about 1.2 km north-east of the house; the coordinates used here are those the Jorasanko Thakur Bari article gives, 22 degrees 35 minutes 06 seconds north, 88 degrees 21 minutes 33 seconds east.
stops.campa: The youngest surviving son of Debendranath Tagore and Sarada Devi is born in the family mansion at Jorasanko, in the north of Calcutta, a house rich for three generations and reforming for two. His father is called the Maharshi and leads the Brahmo Samaj, the monotheist reform current of Bengal. His brothers paint, compose, edit magazines and stage plays in the courtyard, so that the Bengal Renaissance is not a movement the child will later join but the ordinary noise of the rooms he is born into. He is given no schooling he can bear, and is taught at home.
suggested_refs: Jorasanko Thakur Bari, north Kolkata, the house of his birth, his marriage, and his death

stops.name: Santiniketan, Birbhum: the red earth his father bought
stops.date_confidence: the journey is attested for 1873, following his upanayana at about eleven; the month is inferred to order the segment. Debendranath's purchase of the Bhubandanga land in Birbhum in 1867 and his building of the prayer hall are attested on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debendranath_Tagore. The pin is the canonical Santiniketan coordinate already in use in this corpus.
stops.campa: At about eleven he is invested with the sacred thread, and his father takes him out of the house on a journey that will run for months. They stop first on the tract of red laterite in Birbhum that Debendranath bought in 1867 and named Santiniketan, the abode of peace: a prayer hall, a few trees, open country in every direction. The boy is set to recite Sanskrit and to watch the sky after dark. Nothing here is built for children. He will come back at forty and put a school on it.
suggested_refs: The prayer hall (Upasana Griha) built by Debendranath Tagore at Santiniketan

stops.name: Amritsar, the singing at the Golden Temple
stops.date_confidence: the 1873 visit to Amritsar with his father is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the month is inferred to order the segment.
stops.campa: Father and son come to Amritsar and to the Harmandir Sahib, where the Sikh singers keep the shabad going above the water from before dawn. The boy is taken to listen, and it stays with him: devotional music belonging neither to his family's Brahmo monotheism nor to the temple Hinduism his father had reformed away from. Debendranath has him learn some of the hymns by heart. He is eleven years old and out of Calcutta for the first time in his life.
suggested_refs: Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar, and the continuous kirtan he heard there in 1873

stops.name: Dalhousie, the Upanishads on the hill
stops.date_confidence: the stay at Dalhousie in 1873 and the subjects studied are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the month is inferred to order the segment.
stops.campa: They climb to the hill station in the Himalaya and take a house. Before daylight his father wakes him for Sanskrit; the days go to history, biography, astronomy, and the Upanishads read aloud in the mountain air by a man who has arranged his entire life around them. Between lessons the boy has the hillside to himself. Debendranath will not have him schooled by strangers and will not have him idle. These months are the only sustained education Rabindranath ever receives.
suggested_refs: The Upanishadic reading Debendranath Tagore made the core of Brahmo practice

segments.name: England, and the House He Came Back To

stops.name: Medina Villas, Brighton and Hove: sent to be a barrister
stops.date_confidence: the 1878 stay near Brighton with his brother Satyendranath's family and the brief public-school attendance are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the month is inferred. The pin is corrected: the pool's geography lens carried -0.159, about 1.1 km east of the street; OpenStreetMap places Medina Villas, Hove BN3, at 50.8258, -0.1742.
stops.campa: At sixteen he had printed faux-medieval Vaishnava lyrics signed Bhanusimha, and readers had taken them for a rediscovered poet of some earlier century; the same year he published Bhikharini, called since the first short story written in Bengali. At seventeen the family sends him to England to become a barrister. He lodges near Brighton with the household of his brother Satyendranath, the first Indian in the Indian Civil Service, and is put into a local public school for a matter of weeks. The sea is grey and the classroom is cold.
suggested_refs: The Bhanusimha Thakurer Padabali, the pseudonymous cycle of 1877

stops.name: University College London, Gower Street: the degree not taken
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1878-1880 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore), including Henry Morley's lectures and the departure without a degree; the day and month are placeholders inside the attested range.
stops.campa: In London he enrols at University College and goes to Henry Morley's lectures on English literature, which he likes, and reads law, which he does not. He learns English and Irish tunes in boarding houses, argues about Shakespeare, and sends home letters so severe about English manners that the family magazine prints them and the family is embarrassed. He takes no degree and no call to the bar. In 1880 his father sends for him and he returns to Calcutta with nothing to show but an ear for another country's music.
suggested_refs: Henry Morley's UCL lectures on English literature, 1878-1880

stops.name: Jorasanko, the marriage to Bhabatarini
stops.date_confidence: attested: 9 December 1883, 24 Agrahayana 1290 BS (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrinalini_Devi). The pool's chronology lens said the bride was 'about ten'; the Mrinalini Devi article says nine, born 1874, married while Tagore was twenty-two, and gives her home as Phultala in what was then Jessore district, now Khulna in Bangladesh. Dakshindihi is the hamlet within Phultala.
stops.campa: He is twenty-two. The bride, Bhabatarini, is nine, from Phultala in Jessore district, chosen because the family needed a girl of their own Pirali Brahmin line and the choices were few. She is renamed Mrinalini Devi and set to lessons. Nothing in the arrangement is unusual for elite Bengal in 1883, and nothing in it was chosen by either of them. They will have five children. He will not marry again after her death, and the household she runs, on the river estates and later at the school, is the ground under two decades of his work.
suggested_refs: Dakshindihi, Phultala, Khulna: the bride's family house, now a Tagore memorial

stops.name: Jorasanko, Kadambari
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadambari_Devi): 21 April 1884, four months after the wedding, suicide, opium named. No authenticated note survives and no motive is on the record; everything beyond those facts is family tradition.
stops.campa: Four months after his wedding, Kadambari Devi, the wife of his brother Jyotirindranath, dies by suicide in the house at Jorasanko. She was a year older than he, the first reader of most of what he had written, the woman his early books were addressed to. Opium is named. No authenticated note survives, and the family keeps whatever it knows. He is twenty-three. The biographies build a great deal past those few facts, and none of what they build is on the record; the record offers no motive at all.
suggested_refs: The suppressed papers of the Kadambari Devi inquest, Calcutta, April 1884

stops.name: Kuthibari, Shelaidaha: the poet made a landlord
stops.date_confidence: the 1890 assignment of the zamindari estates is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the day and month are placeholders. Pin corrected: the pool's geography lens carried 23.9053, 89.1962, about 3 km off; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilaidaha gives 23 degrees 55 minutes 12 seconds north, 89 degrees 13 minutes 12 seconds east, in Kumarkhali Upazila, Kushtia District.
stops.campa: His father hands him the family estates and the poet becomes a landlord. He takes the houseboat out onto the Padma and lives aboard for months at a time, hearing rent disputes, boundary quarrels, and the affairs of tenants who have never seen a Tagore before, then writing at night on the deck. The letters he sends his niece Indira from these years, later collected as Chinnapatra, are the record of a man learning his own country at the level of the sandbank and the flooded field. Manasi appears the same year.
suggested_refs: Chinnapatra, the Padma letters to Indira Devi Chaudhurani
The Shelaidaha Kuthibari, now a museum in Kushtia District, Bangladesh

stops.name: Kuthibari, Shahzadpur: the short story invented
stops.date_confidence: the estate management and the composition of much of Galpaguchchha in the 1890s are attested in the standard biography (Dutta and Robinson, The Myriad-Minded Man) and carried by the research dossier; the specific year 1893 is a placeholder inside the attested decade, and the coordinate was not independently re-fetched.
stops.campa: At the estate house at Shahzadpur he collects revenue, hears the villages, and writes the stories later gathered as Galpaguchchha: the postmaster with nobody to write to, the child bride, the clerk, the moneylender's ledger. The form barely exists in Bengali before him, and he is making it out of the paperwork on his own desk. He works in a first-floor room with the district passing beneath the window, close enough to hear it, and he is the landlord of nearly everyone he writes about.
sources: Krishna Dutta and Andrew Robinson, Rabindranath Tagore: The Myriad-Minded Man (1995)
suggested_refs: Galpaguchchha, the collected short stories of the estate years

stops.name: Kuthibari, Patisar: cooperative credit in the rent-roll
stops.date_confidence: the Patisar experiments in cooperative credit, arbitration and village schooling are dossier-sourced and consistent with the standard biography; the year is a placeholder inside the 1890s-1900s range. Pin corrected: the pool carried 24.793, 88.79, roughly 33 km off in open country; OpenStreetMap places Patisar in Raninagar Upazila, Naogaon District, Rajshahi Division, at 24.6731, 89.0801.
stops.campa: At Patisar, in Raninagar, he tries what the other two estates do not see: cooperative credit, arbitration in place of the courts, schooling paid out of the rent. He lends the tenants money at rates that undercut the local usurers and carries the losses himself. He sets up village courts and sends the disputes back to the villages that raised them, which keeps the tenants out of the colonial courts. All of it comes out of his own rent-roll. It is patchy and unfinished when he leaves it.
sources: Krishna Dutta and Andrew Robinson, Rabindranath Tagore: The Myriad-Minded Man (1995)
suggested_refs: The Patisar Kuthibari, Raninagar, Naogaon District, Bangladesh

segments.name: The School in the Mango Grove

stops.name: Santiniketan, the Brahmacharyasrama opened
stops.date_confidence: attested for December 1901 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiniketan); the exact day is not established by the reachable sources and 22 December, the traditional Poush festival date at Santiniketan, is used here to order the segment.
stops.campa: He moves to his father's tract in Birbhum and opens a school with five pupils, one of them his own son. Classes are held under the trees. There are no walls, few books, and no punishment worth the name; the boys and the teachers eat together, and the year turns on seasonal festivals he writes the songs for. He calls it Brahmacharyasrama, after the forest schools of the Upanishads his father read to him at Dalhousie. To pay for it he sells his wife's jewellery and the copyrights of his books, and he teaches most of the classes himself.
suggested_refs: The Patha Bhavana open-air classrooms at Santiniketan

stops.name: Jorasanko, the death of Mrinalini Devi
stops.date_confidence: attested: 23 November 1902, aged 28, at Jorasanko Thakur Bari (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrinalini_Devi). The pool's chronology lens placed the death at Santiniketan and was wrong; she fell ill there and was brought to the Calcutta house. The appendicitis suggestion is their son Rathindranath's later opinion, not a diagnosis.
stops.campa: She falls ill at the school and is carried down to Calcutta, to the house where he was born. He nurses her for two months in an upstairs room, fanning her through the nights himself, and she dies there at twenty-eight of an illness nobody names. Their eldest son will say later that he believed it was appendicitis. Rabindranath is forty-one, with five children and a school with no money. He writes a book of short poems for her that year and goes back to Birbhum.
suggested_refs: Smaran (1903), the sequence written after Mrinalini Devi's death

stops.name: Calcutta, the death of the Maharshi
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the city: Debendranath Tagore died 19 January 1905 at Calcutta, aged 87 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debendranath_Tagore). That the death occurred inside the Jorasanko mansion is not stated by that source; only 'Calcutta' is sourced, and the Jorasanko pin is used here for want of a narrower one.
stops.campa: The Maharshi dies at eighty-seven, and the Brahmo Samaj loses the man who had held it together for half a century. He had bought the Birbhum land in 1867, built the prayer hall, and set the ground aside for a retreat; his son has since put a school on it and cannot pay for it. What passes to Rabindranath is the estates, the debts, and the authority of the family name in Bengal. He is forty-three, and for the first time there is nobody above him in the house.
suggested_refs: Debendranath Tagore's Brahmo Dharma and the Adi Brahmo Samaj he led

stops.name: Calcutta, the song and the King-Emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jana_Gana_Mana): composed 11 December 1911, first sung 27 December 1911 at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress, with a separate song honouring the visiting King George V performed the same day. The Beadon Square session pin is the pool's geography lens value and was not independently verified.
stops.campa: He writes the song on the eleventh of December, five stanzas in Sanskritized Bengali addressed to the Bharata Bhagya Bidhata, the dispenser of India's destiny. On the twenty-seventh it is sung at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. George V is in the country for the Delhi Durbar and a separate loyal song is performed the same day. The English press conflates the two, and the story that Tagore had hymned an emperor begins a career of its own that outlives every man in the room. He will still be denying it in a letter twenty-six years later.
suggested_refs: Tagore's own 1937 letter to Pulin Bihari Sen denying that the song honoured the King-Emperor

segments.name: Gitanjali, and a Prize Read Out in His Absence

stops.name: Shelaidaha, the notebook of English prose
stops.date_confidence: attested that he began the English Gitanjali at Shelaidaha in 1912 while recovering from illness before the voyage (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilaidaha; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gitanjali); the month is inferred to order the segment.
stops.campa: Ill, and ordered to rest before a voyage to England, he goes back to the river house and, with nothing else to do, begins turning his own Bengali poems into English prose. He is not translating so much as making a second and quieter thing: he cuts, he fuses two poems into one, he drops the metre and lets the sentences go flat and biblical. He carries the notebook aboard ship and works at it crossing the Arabian Sea, and again in a Bloomsbury lodging when he lands. He is fifty-one and unknown outside Bengal.
stops.quote: Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life.
stops.quote_source: Gitanjali (1912), poem I, Tagore's own English version; text confirmed on en.wikisource.org/wiki/Gitanjali/1
suggested_refs: The 1910 Bengali Gitanjali, from which fifty-three of the English poems derive

stops.name: London, the India Society edition
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1912, the India Society of London, 103 prose poems, Yeats's introduction, Rothenstein's circulation of the manuscript (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gitanjali). The pin is the canonical London coordinate used across this corpus: no reachable source gives the India Society's office address, and the pool's geography lens carried an unattributed pin near the Strand.
stops.campa: The painter William Rothenstein reads the notebook and passes it round literary London. W. B. Yeats takes it home, carries it about with him for weeks, reads it on trains and in restaurants, and writes an introduction saying the prose has stirred his blood as nothing has for years. Ezra Pound is among the first to hear the poems read aloud. In November the India Society prints Gitanjali: Song Offerings, a hundred and three prose pieces drawn from a dozen Bengali books, two of them fused into one. The book that makes him world-famous is one no Bengali reader has ever seen.
stops.quote: ...these prose translations from Rabindranath Tagore have stirred my blood as nothing has for years...
stops.quote_source: W. B. Yeats, Introduction to Gitanjali, September 1912; quoted with leading and trailing ellipsis because the sentence in the original begins 'But though these prose translations...' (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Gitanjali/Introduction)
suggested_refs: Gitanjali: Song Offerings (India Society, November 1912), with Yeats's introduction
William Rothenstein's portraits and letters concerning the 1912 manuscript

stops.name: Santiniketan, the news out of Stockholm
stops.date_confidence: attested that he learned of the prize in November 1913 in Bengal and did not travel to Stockholm (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore; research dossier). The precise day the news reached him is not established; 14 November, the Academy's announcement date, is used to order the segment. The Academy's citation wording is carried from the widely reproduced text and not from a page fetched in this pass, since nobelprize.org returned 403.
stops.campa: The news reaches Bengal by telegram: the Swedish Academy has given him the prize in literature, the first it has given to anyone outside Europe. He is at the school. The message is read out to a crowd that comes down from Calcutta by train and carriage to congratulate him, some of whom, he notices, had not troubled to read him before Stockholm did. He does not go to the ceremony. The British minister to Sweden reads his message at the banquet in his place, and the medal arrives at Santiniketan by post.
stops.quote: because of his profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse, by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West
stops.quote_source: Swedish Academy citation, Nobel Prize in Literature 1913, as widely reproduced; nobelprize.org could not be fetched in the research pass and the wording is therefore carried, not verified
suggested_refs: Thomas Sturge Moore's 1913 nomination of Tagore to the Swedish Academy
The 1913 Nobel banquet message read on his behalf by the British minister

stops.name: Calcutta, the knighthood
stops.date_confidence: attested that George V made him a Knight Bachelor in the 1915 Birthday Honours (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the day is the Birthday Honours date and his own whereabouts that week are not established. That Gandhi called him Gurudev is not documented on any page reached in the research pass and stays a reconstruction. The claim that Tagore coined 'Mahatma' is not merely unprovable but weighed against: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma dates his use to 6 March 1915 and cites two earlier written uses, Pranjivan Mehta's 1909 letter to Gokhale and a Jetpur document of 21 January 1915.
stops.campa: George V makes him a Knight Bachelor in the birthday honours, and the poet who has spent a decade attacking the idea of the nation becomes Sir Rabindranath. He accepts it. Gandhi has been back from South Africa since January and the two are already circling each other in print, the poet against the machine of nationalism, the lawyer building one; each is credited with naming the other, Gurudev on one side and Mahatma on the other, and the documents do not support the second attribution. The knighthood lasts four years.
suggested_refs: The 1915 Birthday Honours list
The Tagore-Gandhi correspondence on nationalism, the charkha, and non-cooperation

stops.name: Tokyo, the lectures against the Nation
stops.date_confidence: the 1916 Japan lectures and the resulting book Nationalism are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the month is inferred to order the segment.
stops.campa: He lectures across Japan on what he calls the Nation: the organized power of a people arranged for a mechanical purpose, which he tells his hosts they have imported from the West along with the ships and the guns. The halls are full and the welcome cools as he goes on. Japanese admirers who had received an Asian laureate as the voice of a rising East find him arguing that the East is being ruined by precisely what raises it. The lectures become the book Nationalism the following year.
stops.quote: A nation, in the sense of the political and economic union of a people, is that aspect which a whole population assumes when organized for a mechanical purpose.
stops.quote_source: Nationalism (1917), lecture 'Nationalism in the West'; Project Gutenberg ebook 40766
suggested_refs: Nationalism (Macmillan, 1917), the three lectures and 'The Sunset of the Century'

segments.name: The Knighthood Returned, the University Founded

stops.name: Santiniketan, the foundation stone of Visva-Bharati
stops.date_confidence: attested: 24 December 1918, 8 Poush 1325 in the Bengali calendar (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visva-Bharati_University).
stops.campa: On the eighth of Poush he lays the foundation stone of a university on the school ground and gives it a name meaning the world in one nest: Visva-Bharati. What he intends is a place where India is not taught defensively, where Chinese and Persian and Tibetan and European learning sit down in the same compound, and where a student takes a craft, a language and a season's festival together. He has no endowment. He has the prize money, the copyrights, the estates, and a talent for raising funds by lecturing in countries he criticizes.
suggested_refs: Cheena Bhavana and the Persian and Islamic studies departments of Visva-Bharati

stops.name: Calcutta, the letter to Lord Chelmsford
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jallianwala_Bagh_massacre): the massacre at Amritsar on 13 April 1919, the renunciation letter to Viceroy Lord Chelmsford dated 31 May 1919. The stop is placed at Calcutta, where the letter was written, not at Jallianwala Bagh: Tagore was not at Amritsar in 1919, and the massacre site is a stop on Gandhi's own file. That Chelmsford never formally accepted the renunciation is traditional and was not verified in this pass.
stops.campa: Six weeks after Dyer's troops fire into a walled garden at Amritsar and kill hundreds of people who cannot get out, and after the censorship lifts enough for Bengal to learn the size of it, he sits up through the night and writes to the Viceroy renouncing his knighthood. He asks that the badge be taken back so that he may stand shorn of all special distinctions beside those of his countrymen held liable to a degradation not fit for human beings. No other Indian holder of an imperial honour signs with him. The letter is dated the thirty-first of May 1919.
stops.quote: The time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring in their incongruous context of humiliation, and I for my part wish to stand, shorn of all special distinctions, by the side of my countrymen.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Viceroy Lord Chelmsford, 31 May 1919, as reproduced in English Writings of Rabindranath Tagore vol. 8 and quoted on en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jallianwala_Bagh_massacre
suggested_refs: Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, 13 April 1919, the massacre the letter answers
The full text of the Chelmsford letter in English Writings of Rabindranath Tagore, vol. 8

stops.name: Darmstadt, the Tagore Week at the School of Wisdom
stops.date_confidence: attested from within this corpus: keyserling.journey.json dates the Tagore-Woche at the School of Wisdom to 9-14 June 1921 and names the circle, corroborated by martin_buber.journey.json's Darmstadt stop. Keyserling had sought Tagore out in Calcutta on his own round-the-world journey, per the same file.
stops.campa: Count Hermann Keyserling, who had sought him out in Calcutta on his own journey round the world, gives over a whole week of his School of Wisdom to him. He is on the continent to raise money for a university, and Germany gives him crowds. For six days in June he reads and speaks to an audience that has lost a war and an emperor and is looking east for something to live by. Carl Jung is in the room, and Max Scheler, Hans Driesch, Leo Frobenius, and Richard Wilhelm, who is at work on the I Ching.
sources: martin_buber.journey.json, Darmstadt School of Wisdom stop
suggested_refs: Hedwig Lachmann's German translations of Tagore, made in the Landauer household at Hermsdorf

stops.name: Santiniketan, Visva-Bharati inaugurated
stops.date_confidence: the formal establishment in 1921 is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visva-Bharati_University); the exact December day is a reconstruction used to order the segment. Tucci's arrival is dated from giuseppe_tucci.journey.json: he sailed for India in November 1925 and taught at Santiniketan for five and a half years.
stops.campa: The university opens formally. He makes over to it the income of the estates, his copyrights, and the prize money, and keeps for himself only the obligation to raise the rest. Scholars begin arriving from outside: Giuseppe Tucci sails from Italy in 1925 and stays five and a half years, teaching Italian and Chinese in mud-walled classrooms under the trees. The place is broke in its first year and stays broke. He is sixty, and from now on he travels to pay for it.
suggested_refs: The deed transferring Tagore's copyrights and estate income to Visva-Bharati

stops.name: Surul, the Institute of Rural Reconstruction
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1922, in the manor house at Surul, with Leonard Knight Elmhirst as first director (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sriniketan); Elmhirst had returned to India as Tagore's secretary in November 1921. The day and month are placeholders. The funder must be named Dorothy Whitney Straight: she did not marry Elmhirst until September 1925, so 'Dorothy Straight Elmhirst' is anachronistic for 1922. Pin corrected from the pool's 23.65, 87.63, about 4 km off, to the OpenStreetMap coordinate for Surul.
stops.campa: Two miles from the school, in a manor house at Surul, he starts an Institute of Rural Reconstruction and puts an English agricultural economist in charge of it. Leonard Elmhirst had come out to India as his secretary the year before; the money comes from Dorothy Whitney Straight, an American widow Elmhirst will marry in 1925. The institute runs demonstration plots and cooperatives, a health service, weaving and tanning shops, and a school for village children. Twenty-six years after the experiment in the Patisar rent-roll, the idea has an address and a director.
suggested_refs: Sriniketan's demonstration farm and cooperative records, 1922 onward
Dartington Hall, the English institution Elmhirst and Whitney Straight founded on the Sriniketan model
The agricultural training of his son Rathindranath Tagore and Santosh Chandra Majumdar at the University of Illinois, graduating 1909, which Tagore arranged for this work

segments.name: The Ship That Stopped at Buenos Aires, and the Italy After

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the forced landing
stops.date_confidence: attested: arrival 6 November 1924, the Peru visit abandoned through illness (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore). es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Ocampo adds that he lodged first at the Plaza Hotel, then convalesced at Miralrio, a quinta Ocampo borrowed from her cousin's husband and afterwards had to rent when the intended eight-day stay became two months. The disembarkation pin is inherited unchanged from victoria_ocampo.journey.json.
stops.campa: The ship carrying him to Peru, where a centenary of independence wants a poet, puts in at Buenos Aires with the poet ill: influenza caught mid-ocean, and a heart his doctors will not risk on the Andes. He is sixty-three and has never been to South America. He goes ashore into a country he had not meant to visit, and within days Victoria Ocampo, thirty-four years old and a reader of his since Gitanjali, has taken charge of him: a hotel first, then a house on the bluff at San Isidro, borrowed from a cousin's husband and afterwards rented when the eight days become two months.
suggested_refs: The port of Buenos Aires, where the ship to Lima was forced to dock

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Miralrio
stops.date_confidence: traditional for the exact day of the move, which is not established; the two-month convalescence at Miralrio is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Ocampo). The pin is inherited byte-for-byte from victoria_ocampo.journey.json's San Isidro stops; it is the bluff, not the villa's plot, and the house itself has since been demolished.
stops.campa: Miralrio stands above the Plata among the barrancas, and he spends two months on its terrace watching a river as wide as a sea. Ocampo furnishes the house at her own expense, brings him fruit, and defends him from a Buenos Aires society eager to lionize a sick man. He writes in Bengali again for the first time in months and translates some of it for her on the spot, because she reads no Bengali and will not wait. He gives her a Sanskrit name, Vijaya, which is her own name in another language, and calls her nothing else for the rest of his life.

Victoria Ocampo, Tagore en las barrancas de San Isidro (1961)

stops.name: San Isidro, the departure and the dedication of Purabi
stops.date_confidence: attested: departure 4 January 1925 (es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Ocampo). The dedication of Purabi to 'Vijaya' and the claim that it is his only book dedicated outside his family and country are dossier-sourced and carried by victoria_ocampo.journey.json; that page does not carry the dedication.
stops.campa: He sails on the fourth of January, never having got to Peru. Back in Bengal he gathers the poems written on that terrace into a book he calls Purabi, after an evening raga, and dedicates the whole of it to Vijaya, the name he had given her at Miralrio: the only book of his dedicated to anyone outside his family and his country. They meet once more, in Paris in 1930, and write to each other until he dies. She keeps the chair he sat in and shows it to visitors for fifty years.
suggested_refs: Purabi (1925), dedicated in full to 'Vijaya'
The Tagore-Ocampo correspondence, edited by Ketaki Kushari Dyson

stops.name: Rome, the guest of the regime
stops.date_confidence: the 1926 Italian tour, the arrival at Naples, and the meeting with Mussolini are attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the exact date of the Rome meeting was not established in the research pass. The repudiation letter in the Manchester Guardian of 5 August 1926 and Romain Rolland's part in supplying evidence are carried from the dossier and standard scholarship, and were not confirmed by a fetched source; they are placed in this stop rather than in Manchester, where Tagore was not.
stops.campa: Invited by the Italian government, welcomed at Naples, moved through an itinerary the regime controls and translated by men the regime supplies, he meets Mussolini in Rome and says courteous things about a country whose newspapers he cannot read. The Fascist press prints the courtesies as endorsement and circulates them across Europe. Romain Rolland and Italian exiles reach him afterwards with the evidence of what the regime does at home, and on the fifth of August he publishes a repudiation in the Manchester Guardian. The retraction travels a great deal less far than the praise did.
suggested_refs: Tagore's letter of 5 August 1926 in the Manchester Guardian
Romain Rolland's correspondence on the Italian tour

stops.name: Balatonfured, the heart and the lake
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was received for heart treatment at the state cardiology hospital at Balatonfured during the 1926 European tour, that India gave a bust in 1956 sculpted by Rasithan Kashar, that a new statue replaced it in 2005, and that the promenade has carried his name since 1957 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balatonfured; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore). The month is inferred. The lime tree he is said to have planted in the grounds is famous locally but was not confirmed by any source reached in the research pass.
stops.campa: His heart gives out on the tour and he is taken to the state cardiology hospital on the north shore of Lake Balaton, where a Hungarian doctor puts him to bed for weeks. Local memory has him planting a lime tree in the grounds once he is able to walk. The town names its lakeside promenade for him in 1957, sixteen years after his death. India sends a bust in 1956, and a better one to replace it in 2005. He had been in the town a matter of weeks, and in bed for most of them.

stops.name: Borobudur, Java: the stone crossing
stops.date_confidence: the four-month Southeast Asia tour of 1927 with Suniti Kumar Chatterji, opening at Singapore in July and taking in Java and Bali, is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore); the month of the Borobudur visit is inferred. Java-Jatrir Patra as the resulting book is dossier-sourced.
stops.campa: He opens a four-month tour of Southeast Asia at Singapore with the linguist Suniti Kumar Chatterji and works east through Java to the great stupa on the plain, where the reliefs run for miles around the terraces and the Buddha sits in stone that Indian hands did not cut but Indian thought arranged. He is after the old passage: what went from India to the archipelago before Europe went anywhere, and what came back. The tour goes on to Bali. He writes it up as Java-Jatrir Patra, letters of a traveler to Java.

stops.name: Paris, the paintings hung
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the exhibition itself: victoria_ocampo.journey.json attests only that Tagore and Ocampo met again in France in 1930, and the Paris exhibition of his paintings arranged by her is dossier-sourced, not independently confirmed. The day is a placeholder. The pin is the canonical Paris coordinate used across this corpus.
stops.campa: At sixty-nine he has begun to draw. The crossings-out in his manuscripts had been running into shapes, birds, faces, creatures nobody can name, and he has let them become pictures. Victoria Ocampo, who has not seen him since San Isidro, arranges an exhibition in Paris, so that the paintings hang in a European gallery before any Indian one shows them. Critics who came for a mystic find something dark, unschooled and modern. It is the second and last time the two of them are in the same room.

stops.name: Manchester College, Oxford: the Hibbert Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Hibbert Lectures were delivered at Oxford in May 1930 and published in 1931 as The Religion of Man (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Religion_of_Man); the exact day is not established. Venue corrected: the pool's geography lens pinned the Sheldonian Theatre, but the Hibbert series is hosted by Manchester College, today Harris Manchester College on Mansfield Road, whose coordinate is used here.
stops.campa: He gives the Hibbert Lectures at the Unitarian college that hosts the series, and the argument is the one he has been making since the school opened in the mango grove: that the divine is not reached by leaving the human, that God is met in the relation between persons rather than above it. The lectures are printed the next year as The Religion of Man, with an appendix that has nothing to do with religion at all, a conversation held in July with a physicist outside Berlin.
suggested_refs: The Religion of Man (Macmillan, 1931), the Hibbert Lectures with their appendix

stops.name: Caputh, the afternoon with Einstein
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not silently resolved: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore dates the recorded conversation 14 April 1930, while the standard scholarly record and themarginalian.org's direct quotation of the transcript give 14 July 1930 at Einstein's summer house. July is used here because April is impossible on the 1930 itinerary, in which the Oxford Hibbert Lectures fall in May and Germany follows. Pin corrected from the pool's 52.366, 12.955 to the Caputh village coordinate given by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caputh,_Brandenburg; the house itself stands at Am Waldrand, just south of the village centre. This corpus's einstein.journey.json carries no Tagore stop.
stops.campa: Einstein's summer house at Caputh is a year old, wooden, built for him by Konrad Wachsmann in a stand of pines outside Potsdam, and he will be driven out of it in three years. On the fourteenth of July the poet comes and they talk, with a stenographer present, about whether truth is independent of humanity. Einstein holds that the table is there whether or not anyone is in the room. Tagore holds that a table, as anything sayable, is a table for minds. Neither moves. The transcript goes into a book on religion, and a century of retelling flattens it into scientist against mystic.
suggested_refs: 'Note on the Nature of Reality', appendix to The Religion of Man (1931)

stops.name: Tehran, the guest of the Shah
stops.date_confidence: the 1932 visit to Iran at Reza Shah Pahlavi's invitation is attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore), with the continuation into Iraq and the meeting with Bedouin tagged as reconstruction in the research pool. The exact day is a placeholder. That a plane was sent for him and that he read at Hafez's tomb are traditional and were not confirmed by any source reached in the research pass.
stops.campa: Reza Shah invites him, and at seventy he flies for the first time in his life, over the Gulf into Bushehr and on to Tehran and Shiraz. He is received as the guest of a state busy inventing its own modernity, and says of Persia what he has been saying of Japan and of Italy in another key: that the soul of a people is not the same thing as its government. It is the last of his long journeys west. From Iran he crosses into Iraq and sits with Bedouin in the desert, carried most of the way.

stops.name: Santiniketan, the Frenchwoman who takes a Hindu name
stops.date_confidence: attested from within this corpus: savitri_devi.journey.json dates the meeting at Shantiniketan to July 1935 and the conversion and renaming to the same visit. The pin is the canonical Santiniketan coordinate that file uses.
stops.campa: A Greek-French woman of thirty, Maximiani Portas, arrives at the ashram in July, travelling to find in Hinduism the pagan Europe she believes Christianity destroyed. She meets him, converts formally, and takes the name Savitri Devi. Visva-Bharati has become a place foreigners come to be changed by and it does not screen them; he is seventy-four and receives whoever arrives. She will carry the name for the rest of her life, into a career of Aryan mythmaking and open Hitler-worship that ends a long way from anything taught in this compound.

stops.name: Santiniketan, the first collapse
stops.date_confidence: the sourced wording is 'late 1937': en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore says he lost consciousness and remained comatose and near death for a time. The research dossier's 'September 1937' is not sourced and is not used; November is a placeholder for ordering within 'late 1937'. The same article records a second and worse collapse at the end of 1940 from which he never recovered. Bose's dedication of Visva-Parichay to Tagore in 1937 and his later vice-chancellorship of Visva-Bharati are attested in satyendra_nath_bose.journey.json.
stops.campa: Late in the year he loses consciousness at Santiniketan and lies comatose, near death, for a stretch nobody can shorten. He comes back from it and goes on working: the poems get shorter and harder, and the songs and the paintings keep coming. In the same year the physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, who has written the first popular science book in Bengali, dedicates it to him; Bose will one day be vice-chancellor of this university. A second collapse comes at the end of 1940, and from that one he does not return.
suggested_refs: Visva-Parichay (1937), dedicated by Satyendra Nath Bose to Tagore

stops.name: Jorasanko, the last poem dictated
stops.date_confidence: attested: he dictated his last poem on 30 July 1941, the day before a scheduled operation (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore).
stops.campa: He is brought down from Santiniketan to the house at Jorasanko for an operation on a urinary obstruction he had refused surgery for. They will cut in an upstairs room of the house he was born in eighty years earlier, and the surgery will not save him. On the thirtieth of July, the day before, he dictates a poem, because he can no longer hold a pen. It is his last. It is about the deceptions the world puts in the path of a man who has gone on believing in it.
suggested_refs: 'Tomar srishtir path', the poem dictated on 30 July 1941

stops.name: Jorasanko, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: 7 August 1941 at the Jorasanko mansion, aged eighty, following complications of a urinary and prostatic illness treated surgically; no autopsy-based diagnosis exists (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabindranath_Tagore). That the date corresponds to 22 Srabon in the Bengali calendar is the universal Bengali usage but was not verified against a fetched source in the research pass.
stops.campa: He dies on the seventh of August, twenty-two Srabon by the calendar Bengal actually keeps, in the room he was born in eighty years and three months earlier. There is no modern diagnosis and none was sought. He has written some two thousand songs and the country sings them without always knowing whose they are; it has been reading him for sixty years. The day of his death becomes a date in the Bengali year, marked with the songs rather than with prayers.
stops.quote: I have got my leave. Bid me farewell, my brothers! I bow to you all and take my departure.
stops.quote_source: Gitanjali (1912), poem XCIII, Tagore's own English version; Project Gutenberg ebook 7164
suggested_refs: Baishe Srabon, the annual Bengali observance of his death day

stops.name: Nimtala Ghat, the burning
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nimtala_Crematorium states that Tagore was cremated there in 1941 and that a Rabindranath Tagore Memorial stands in the crematorium compound, beautified in a 2010 refurbishment. Pin corrected from the pool's two differing values, 22.596/88.357 and 22.5959/88.3554, to the OpenStreetMap coordinate for Nimtala Ghat on Strand Bank Road. The contemporary accounts of crowd disorder and souvenir-taking around the body vary and are not adjudicated here.
stops.campa: He is carried out of Jorasanko and burned the same day. The body goes through Calcutta to the ghat on the Hooghly in a crowd nobody can count, and the crowd is not orderly: contemporary accounts describe hair pulled from the head and threads taken from the shroud, and they differ enough that no single version can be trusted. A memorial is raised later in the crematorium compound and tidied up in a municipal refurbishment in 2010. There is no grave, and there is no tomb.

stops.name: New Delhi, the first stanza becomes an anthem
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Constituent Assembly adopted the first stanza of Jana Gana Mana on 24 January 1950 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jana_Gana_Mana). For Bangladesh the date must be split: Amar Sonar Bangla was adopted provisionally by the Provisional Government on 10 April 1971 and constitutionally on 16 December 1972 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amar_Sonar_Bangla). The Sri Lanka claim is refuted: Ananda Samarakoon composed Namo Namo Matha himself in 1940, adopted 22 November 1951, and he abandoned his Santiniketan course after six months (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ananda_Samarakoon).
stops.campa: The Constituent Assembly adopts the first stanza of Bharoto Bhagyo Bidhata as the national anthem of the Republic of India, thirty-nine years after it was sung at a Congress session and nine years after the poet's death. In 1971 a song he wrote in Bengali is taken up by a provisional government fighting a war of secession, and Amar Sonar Bangla is written into the constitution of Bangladesh the following year. Two sovereign states stand up for the same man's music. A third is often said to; Sri Lanka's anthem was written by a student of his who left the course after six months.

stops.name: Jorasanko, the house made a museum
stops.date_confidence: attested that Rabindra Bharati University was established in 1961 for the birth centenary and that museum status followed the next year (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorasanko_Thakur_Bari). The day is set to the centenary of his birth by the Gregorian calendar and is an ordering device, not a founding date.
stops.campa: For the centenary of his birth the government of West Bengal founds Rabindra Bharati University in the Jorasanko house and turns the rooms into a museum of the family and of the Bengal Renaissance the family largely was. This is the house of his birth, his marriage, his wife's death, his father's Samaj, his last poem and his death. Visitors walk through a private house that has been made into an argument about a century, and the argument is that the century happened here. The courtyard where his brothers staged plays is shown, and so is the room he died in.

stops.name: Santiniketan, the medal taken from the vault
stops.date_confidence: attested (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1913_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature): theft from the Visva-Bharati vault on 25 March 2004, two replacements supplied by the Swedish Academy on 7 December 2004, one gold and one bronze, and the baul singer Pradip Bauri detained in 2016 on suspicion of assisting the robbers. The contradiction flagged in the research pool is resolved against recovery: the article does not say the medal was recovered, and the original remains missing.

The Swedish Academy sends two replacements in December, one gold and one bronze. In 2016 a baul singer, Pradip Bauri, is detained on suspicion of having helped the thieves. What the vault held was the object that made him legible to Europe, and the one object of his career he did not travel to collect. It has never come back.

Eighty-two years after his death, an experiment in teaching under trees is a protected monument. The citation rests on the idea rather than the architecture, on a place designed against the colonial classroom.

stops.name: Jardin de los Poetas, Palermo: the bust that could not be confirmed
stops.date_confidence: unresolved, and the date is a placeholder for ordering only, carrying no evidential weight: it is set after the 2023 inscription solely to keep the unresolved question last in the file, and asserts nothing about when the bust was placed. QUEUE.md names Tagore as one of the busts in the Jardin de los Poetas and the pin is inherited byte-for-byte from jose_marti.journey.json, which uses the canonical Parque Tres de Febrero coordinate also used for Shevchenko and for Dante. But the afterlife lens could not confirm the bust exists: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosedal_de_Palermo says the garden holds twenty-six busts and the retrievable portion named only nine, Tagore not among them, and the Buenos Aires city pages that would settle it returned 404. Flagged for a follow-up fetch of a Turismo Buenos Aires or La Nacion piece on the full roster.
stops.campa: Among the busts of the Rosedal at Palermo, in the garden of the poets where twenty-six heads stand on plinths under the roses, there is said to be one of him. The nine that a reachable list names are Cervantes, Dante, Marti, Rosalia de Castro and five others, and he is not among the nine. The city he came to by accident, ill, in 1924, and left after two months on a borrowed terrace, is the one South American city that took him for its own. Whether it put his face in bronze in the rose garden is a question the sources do not answer.
